title: DRAMScope: Uncovering DRAM Microarchitecture and Characteristics by Issuing Memory Commands
problem: DRAM manufacturers disclose limited microarchitecture details, hindering understanding of DRAM characteristics and activate-induced bitflips (AIBs) like RowHammer. Previous reverse-engineering studies were misled by inaccurate address mapping and lacked proper understanding of modern DRAM cell structures.
motivation: Precise DRAM microarchitecture information is critical for exploring processing-in-memory, enhancing reliability, and mitigating security vulnerabilities.
method: The researchers use three measurement techniques to reverse-engineer DRAM: activate-induced bitflips (when repeated memory access causes data corruption), retention time tests (measuring how long data survives without refresh), and RowCopy (a row-copying technique). They first map DRAM's large-scale organization—subarray sizes, structure, and memory array tiles (MAT, the blocks that form the memory grid)—then examine how bitflips occur at the cell level, using 6F² cell geometry (a description of how cells are laid out in the memory) to identify patterns of accelerated corruption and reveal protection strategies.
key_novelty: Using three complementary measurement techniques to accurately reverse-engineer commercial DRAM and discover previously unknown vulnerabilities to bitflips (data corruption in memory systems) and the specific patterns that cause them to accelerate.
contributions: Accurate DRAM reverse-engineering methodology using three complementary tools (AIBs, retention time test, RowCopy) for validation
Detailed characterization of modern DRAM microarchitecture including subarray, MAT, and row structures
Discovery of new data patterns that accelerate activate-induced bitflips
Identification of previously unknown AIB vulnerabilities and a simple, effective protection solution

metrics.other: DRAM characterization parameters including subarray dimensions, MAT structure, cell layout patterns, AIB acceleration conditions
